_note: Conservative, general-knowledge statements only. Review before enabling and add your own resorts. Each note must be something you can verify.

resorts.name: Zermatt
notes: The village is car-free and sits at the foot of the Matterhorn.
The ski area is linked with Cervinia in Italy.
Glacier terrain extends skiing deep into the season.

resorts.name: Chamonix
notes: The town lies at the foot of Mont Blanc, the highest mountain in the Alps.
The Aiguille du Midi cable car climbs from the valley to a summit station at roughly 3,800 m.
Chamonix hosted the first Winter Olympics in 1924.

resorts.name: St. Anton am Arlberg
notes: St. Anton is the birthplace of the Arlberg technique, an influential early method of teaching alpine skiing.
The resort is known for demanding off-piste terrain and a lively après-ski scene.

resorts.name: Niseko
notes: Niseko is famous for its light, dry powder snow.
Niseko United links four resort areas on the slopes of Mt. Niseko-Annupuri.

resorts.name: Whistler Blackcomb
notes: Whistler Blackcomb hosted the alpine skiing events of the 2010 Winter Olympics.
The Peak 2 Peak Gondola connects Whistler Mountain with Blackcomb Mountain.

resorts.name: Cortina d'Ampezzo
notes: Cortina hosted the 1956 Winter Olympics and was a co-host of the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics.
It lies in the Dolomites, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

resorts.name: Aspen Snowmass
notes: The Aspen Snowmass area is made up of four mountains: Aspen Mountain, Aspen Highlands, Buttermilk and Snowmass.

resorts.name: Kitzbühel
notes: Kitzbühel hosts the Hahnenkamm races each winter, including the famous Streif downhill.
The medieval town centre is a large part of the resort's appeal.

resorts.name: Val Thorens
notes: Val Thorens is often described as the highest ski resort in Europe.
It is part of the Three Valleys, commonly cited as the largest linked ski area in the world.
